toc.title: Mobilized with safety, or without it
An example: a crisis at a high school

sections.title: Giving him space and safety cues

toc.title: Why it worked: my own state

blocks.p: This one is especially for those in helping professions that deal with crises regularly, though it could easily be for parents and teachers as well. I want to talk about high stress jobs and how they might affect our ability to think critically, walk through what's happening through the Polyvagal Theory, and then share an example of a time I was able to defuse a potentially explosive crisis situation at a high school.
One listener, a psychiatric nurse, wrote in with this question:

q: I'm very new to Polyvagal Theory and have started with your podcast. I have a question, though, if you wouldn't mind. I'm a psychiatric nurse in an adult male psychiatric intensive care unit. An awful lot of my 13-hour shifts involve being exposed to very high levels of violence and aggression, sometimes aimed directly at myself, sometimes not. Am I just asking for trouble doing this job by consistently triggering my flight, fight, freeze response? You say how rational thinking goes out the window when you're under threat, but I constantly have to think rationally under threat to keep everyone safe.

blocks.p: Really good question. I feel like I have something to offer here, personally, but also through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory.

Working in a psychiatric ward or a crisis unit, being a police officer, working on an ambulance, nursing: all kinds of jobs involve lots and lots of direct, crisis level, frontline work. I would say even teachers and school counselors deal with crises pretty regularly. In these types of jobs, we have to stay active, and we have to stay mobile. So does that activate our flight or fight state? Absolutely.

I have some direct experience. I worked as a counselor at the Log Cabin Ranch, a non-lockdown juvenile hall facility for San Francisco County. We were called counselors, but really it was more of a guard. When the kids couldn't make it in the regular population of juvenile hall, or their offense was too great, they would send them there. It wasn't locked down, but it was in the middle of nowhere, so if they tried to escape, there was a good chance they would not make it back to civilization. At the time of this episode, I was a therapist in a public school district, and crises happened pretty darn often.

There are also high stress jobs that don't require a lot of mobility. As a school therapist, I sat down for most of the day. I did a lot of one-on-one, sit-down therapy. So a lot of stress, a lot of flight and fight activation, but not a lot of mobility. There were definitely days where I felt like I'd just gotten my butt kicked. It could be draining, but it could also just be activating.

What we want here is not too much defensive activation. We want enough to deal with the situation, but not so much that we're out of our safety state. If we get too far into our defensive state, that means the safety state is inactive. And that is the vagal brake.

Real quick: the vagal brake is the influence of our social engagement system on our heart. When the social engagement system, the ventral vagal pathways, is active, it keeps our heartbeat at a calmer pace. That keeps our defensive behaviors, feelings, sensations, and thoughts more at bay. They get calmed down as long as our vagal brake is active, meaning as long as our safety state, our social engagement system, is on.
Dr. Porges described it simply when he was on the podcast:

q: When you have an efficient vagal brake, if you take it off, your heart rate goes up. If you put it back on, it goes down.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [Dr Stephen Porges: Polyvagal Theory Updates & Critiques (episode 201)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/0e6ffc9f-a364-46e7-bb44-a17299f16de6)

blocks.h: Mobilized with safety, or without it

blocks.p: Being mobilized, or being in a sympathetic state, is not a bad thing in and of itself. It's not necessarily a destructive thing. Having access to those pathways is not even necessarily a defensive thing. It just means they're activated.

As long as the safety state is active, as long as the vagal brake is active, then when we access those more defensive energies, flight, fight, and shutdown, they get repurposed for more prosocial uses. Or we can use a high amount of flight and fight energy for a specific purpose that requires more mobilization. If you have a job where you have to physically restrain a population that is potentially violent toward others, you're going to need a lot of mobilization activated.

But ideally, we have that activation along with our safety pathways being activated as well. If not, then it's just defensive energy. It's just flight or fight. If you're mobilized without the safety state active, the body is just in a flight or fight kind of state, and that's where things can go horribly wrong.

So whether you're working in a psychiatric ward, as a therapist, or as a police officer, you have to have that safety state active. And it's not like a light switch. You don't just turn it off and on. Ideally, it's strong enough to be kind of on at a baseline, just constantly. Another way to put this is that you have a greater window of tolerance. Hopefully your safety state is built up enough that you have more distress tolerance, more resilience. If not, then any of these potentially big crisis situations is going to trigger you into your more mobilized flight and fight energy, and you won't be able to contain it, repurpose it, and use it to deal with the real-life situations that come up.
So is somebody asking for trouble by going into these jobs? Not necessarily. Some of us can do it. It's challenging, but maybe not as much for some as for others.

Mercedes, who used to co-host this podcast, and I were presenting to police officers, and we had a really cool, open discussion with them about how they maintain access to their own safety system and how they don't take things too far, because the job does require a lot of flight and fight energy. And they said, "Look, some of us can handle this, and we're born for this, and some of us just don't belong here."

So I don't think it's necessarily setting yourself up for failure if you go into these types of jobs. It's just: can you handle it or not? You have to be really honest with yourself, in general, but also maybe in that moment before you step into something: can I handle this?
I have said that rational thinking goes out the window when you're under threat, and that's pretty much true. If you don't have access to your safety state, you don't exactly think critically.

You can absolutely be mobilized. You can absolutely be in your flight or fight state and have access to that sympathetic state. But you also have to have access to the top of the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), the safety state. As long as your vagal brake is on, critical thinking is possible. Rational thinking is possible. If the vagal brake is off, meaning the social engagement system is off, then critical thinking is pretty much not going to happen.

So these defensive states are not bad. It's not necessarily a destructive or dysfunctional or maladaptive thing to access them. It just depends on whether you also have access to your safety state at the same time. You have to stay grounded in your safety state.

So let me ask you: what keeps you grounded in your safety state? What helps you feel safe? Whether you're in these jobs or not, you really have to know what keeps you anchored in your social engagement system.

blocks.h: An example: a crisis at a high school

blocks.p: Here's an example of what this can look like. As a school therapist, crises came up pretty often. Sometimes that was sitting one-on-one with a student who came in in some sort of crisis. That year, a lot of panicky things had been coming up for students, more often than in the past, it seemed. But there were also times I was just walking through the campus, something was going on, and they needed a therapist to run in and help out. That came up a handful of times that year alone.

This one time, I was simply leaving my office building, walking through the campus, and I could hear a male voice yelling and screaming, just blowing up. It was a pretty small school, but still, I could hear it all around.

His vagal brake was off. He had lost his capacity to socially engage. He had lost his capacity to feel safe. He was probably in more of a fight state. You could tell by the tone of voice that the intent was to get people to back off, and this was before I even saw him.

He was violating school norms and social norms. That's how you can tell: if you can't follow basic norms, you're probably out of your safety state, and your vagal brake is probably turned off. There was no vocal prosody, no singsongy quality to his voice. You could tell he was in a dysregulated state.

Once I saw him, I could see two security guards attempting to calm him down. I think they were trying to corral him, guide him in a certain direction. What they didn't realize was that they were actually boxing him in. With their bodies, they were reducing his options for where he could go. That increases the flight and fight state, specifically the fight, because if you can't run away, you drop down the polyvagal ladder into the fight state. They had cut off his capacity to escape the situation. Not intentionally, but they had.
That doesn't mean you're actually hitting people. It might mean you're just raising your voice in an attempt to get them to back off, and that's kind of what was happening here.

blocks.h3: Giving him space and safety cues

blocks.p: It didn't feel right to ignore it, so I walked over and asked, "Hey, can I help out?" I made sure to ask security, because I wanted the student to know I was respecting the hierarchy there. Security said, "Yeah, please do." A simple exchange.

At first, they backed off, and I gave the student a lot of distance. I didn't want to increase the pressure of the situation or make him feel more contained than he already was. When you're in flight or fight, you need space. The entire point of flight or fight is to increase space so you can get away and get to safety. And if you can't run away, you actually get closer through aggression, through voice or through physical means, in order to create space, escape, and get to safety.
Then I gave him every cue of safety I could:

ul: Gentle eye contact. I made eye contact with him, direct and focused. I wasn't avoiding it, but I wasn't staring him down, grimacing, making threatening faces, or going wide-eyed. I wanted him to know, "Hey, I'm here. I see you."

Vocal prosody. I wasn't singing, but I used a greater range of voice to show him I was safe. Something like, "Hey, how's it going, man? Are you doing okay? What's going on?" Not sharp, like, "Hey, get back in class," or "What are you doing?"
Open hands. I didn't want my hands hidden. I put them out in the open so he could see: "Hey, I'm safe. Here are my hands. Nothing fishy going on here. I'm not going to surprise you with anything."

Facial affect. No flat face. I was moving my facial muscles, not so much that it was fake, but I wanted him to see my eyebrows moving. I think I was sneaking in some smiles here and there. Not in a mocking way, just, "Hey, what's going on? Are you doing okay? My name's Justin."

blocks.p: I asked him what was going on. I wanted to give him a chance to talk from his point of view. He wasn't running away, and he wasn't fighting me. Right away, he was willing to engage.

At first, he was ranting and yelling about the staff, and that was okay. It wasn't my job to correct him, and I didn't know the reality of the situation anyway. He was still in a fight state, so we had to let that play out. As long as I could give him all my safety cues while he was doing that, it wasn't a big deal. My safety cues could provide co-regulation, which could help him re-regulate, especially if he could voice what he was going through with someone who seemed okay with his intensity and could tolerate it. That can help contain it.

So I didn't argue with him or question him. I just let him vent for a moment, and that ended pretty quickly. All of this was helping me quickly build rapport and safety. The point here is to engage, not to problem solve, and not to get him to do something in particular. I'm just looking for opportunities for connection and simply hearing people out.
By containing him, I don't mean physically. I mean that emotionally, I can tolerate how much emotion you have and be okay with it.

Once I felt we had a connection built up, and it was a pretty rapid build, because I didn't want him staying in the middle of the school yelling, I invited him to walk away from security with me. "Hey, look, why don't we leave this space? Let's go over here. I have a place that's a little more quiet."

It was still out in the open. I didn't think it was a good idea to bring him indoors, especially into my office, which was a lot smaller. It was a nice day, and being outside gave him space to move and fresh air to breathe.

I think that safe leadership quality is a good thing too. I wasn't commanding him. It was, "Hey, I've got you. Emotionally, you're contained. Nothing to stress out about here, as far as you and me. Come on over. Let's talk about this over here."

I kept giving him cues of safety, my full range of voice, but I was also being pretty darn direct: "Hey, man, what's going on? I can see you're upset, and it's okay. Tell me about it." There's some prosody in there, but it's also very direct. Not commanding, more inviting. And I think the fact that I could match his tone of voice without losing control was a signal to him that I was a safe person. So I was matching his energy.

As he was going off about who did what, I paraphrased what he was saying. I wasn't agreeing with him. I was just reflecting: this is what I'm hearing you say. That helps someone feel listened to, and if someone understands him, that can help him calm down as well.

I also validated and normalized his feelings and experiences. That's not about agreeing. At no point did I say, "Yeah, you're right, and you should act that way," or "Yeah, the school messed up." The facts of the situation simply didn't matter in that moment. It was more, "I can see where you're coming from, and I can see why you're reacting that way. It seems like a pretty normal reaction based on what you're telling me."

He told me about what was going on, but he also told me how much stress and pressure he was under. He was going to be the first kid in his family to graduate high school, so there were a lot of expectations on him, and I think most of it he was putting on himself. It meant a lot to him. He knew he had messed around a lot, procrastinated, and missed a lot of school, and it was crunch time: his last couple of weeks to get things done. Plus other family stress and dysfunction, which all the students I met with had some of going on. I don't remember what set the whole thing off, but with all that stress, and now being in a situation where he was making his life worse by yelling, he was probably feeling a lot in that moment.

He wasn't calm, but he was calmer. He was able to lower his voice. He was able to share some eye contact with me here and there. Not sustained, because he wasn't fully accessing a safety state, but it was growing.

While I was talking with him, I knew his mom was on the way. If you work in public schools, you know parents are very loving, we'll say, and they can go off on school staff if they perceive their kids are being mistreated or in some sort of danger. Not a situation you want to be in.

I had no idea who she was or how she'd be. All I knew was that the first thing I wanted for her when she got to the school was to see her son, and see that he was okay. That was another reason I wanted to stay outside. I positioned us right outside the front gate, so that when she arrived, we'd probably see her before she saw us, and we could meet her there. So I was containing his emotions and offering all these cues, plus anticipating what mom was going to need once she arrived.

As a parent, I know I'd want to know what the hell is going on. So as soon as we saw her, I went up to her, introduced myself with the same cues of safety, and right off the bat said, "Hey, this is the situation. This is what's going on." Then the principal came out and started talking with her. I'm not saying she was super happy, but I know the things I did in that situation helped her stay calm enough to not go off on me, the principal, or anybody else.

blocks.h: Why it worked: my own state

blocks.p: This was a kid who didn't really have any behavior problems at the school. He had missed a lot of school, from what he told me, but that was it. And this easily could have gotten a lot worse.

I think a lot of us in these kinds of jobs look for control. We look for containment. We look for compliance. I totally get that. Things go through our minds about safety and interrupting other people's classes, and that's all valid. Security is not always trained on how to effectively deal with these types of situations. It's more about getting it to stop, rather than connecting, building a relationship, and then dealing with the problem. I get that. But there's a lot of validity to building the relationship first, then solving the problem, and then looking for compliance.

I was nervous when I saw this happening. I had no idea who the kid was, what he was capable of, or his history. But it was something I thought I could help with. If I had come from my nervous flight and fight energy, I don't think I would have been helpful. If I hadn't been well regulated in that moment, I probably would have just added to the problem, trying to get him to do what the school as an entity wanted him to do: be quiet and go back to class.

Luckily, I was in my own safe and social state, well regulated, and I was able to offer that to him and help mitigate the situation. If I had come from a flight or fight, control kind of place, it would not have gone well. That's how important it is to remain in your own safety state.

If you have one of these jobs that requires you to be more mobilized, it's more of a challenge. I didn't deal with those situations every day, but I dealt with them often. A lot of my colleagues dealt with them every day. And I'm someone who's well regulated enough that when it comes to these situations, I kind of thrive. I kind of like them, for some reason. In these high crisis situations, I find myself becoming more mobilized, but able to tolerate it and use that energy effectively toward helping someone get back to a baseline, or whatever needs to happen in that moment.

When it comes to these types of jobs, you really have to know yourself and ask yourself, "Is this something I can handle?" Because it will be draining. These jobs will absolutely test your capacity to stay in your safety state.

So are you asking for trouble? If you're not prepared for it, absolutely. But if you know this is something you can handle, stay well regulated, recover from it at the end of the day, and do it all over again, that's your call. I don't know if you're asking for trouble at that point, but you're definitely asking to test what you can handle, and I don't think that's for everybody.
